body.text: Late last month, Pakistan announced that Taiwanese airlines such as China Airlines and EVA Air would not be allowed to fly over the country. This took place after an announcement by Minister of Defense Khawaja Asif, whose responsibilities also entail overflight privileges. Asif claimed that the ban was on the basis of Pakistan’s One China policy.

It was the first time that a country had revoked overflight privileges for Taiwanese airlines on the basis of a claimed One China policy. Previously, EVA Air and China Airlines – which, despite its name, is Taiwan’s national carrier, not to be confused with the Chinese flag carrier Air China – had been cleared for overflight privileges by Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority from October 28 of this year through March 27, 2027.
The move by Pakistan did not last long, however, with the country reversing course soon after. Taiwanese airlines continue to enjoy overflight privileges to Pakistan.

It remains unclear why the decision was made by Pakistan’s government in the first place – and why it was reversed shortly after. It is possible that Pakistan did not anticipate international pressure after the announcement which may have occurred behind the scenes. Likewise, it is not clear as to whether it was the Pakistan government’s decision to revoke Taiwan’s overflight privileges or whether this came after a request from Beijing.

The move came about a month ahead of Taiwan’s local elections in late November. In other countries, China is indeed seeking to apply pressure to Taiwan in the lead-up to the polls. In past months, there have been reports of Taiwanese nationals being denied admittance to Uganda and Kenya, on the basis that their Taiwanese passports were not issued by Beijing, and thus not considered valid travel documents.

In August, four Taiwanese in Uganda had their passports confiscated, though eventually they were returned. In June, two Taiwanese delegates to the 11th Our Ocean Conference in Mombasa, Kenya, were refused admittance to the conference because their Taiwanese passports were considered “invalid.” They subsequently had their passports and cell phones confiscated and were detained for 20 hours, though they were later released. Despite conflicting reports afterward, it appears Taiwanese are still able to enter Kenya using their passports.

Pakistan may have been the first to threaten a wholesale ban on Taiwanese airlines overflying its airspace, but other countries have revoked overflight privileges to specific Taiwanese aircraft, apparently at China’s behest. In April, a trip by President Lai Ching-te to Eswatini, Taiwan’s only African diplomatic ally, was abruptly cancelled. Lai had planned to visit Eswatini for the 40th anniversary of King Mswati III’s accession to the throne, which also marked Mswati’s 58th birthday. The trip was cancelled after Madagascar, Mauritius, and the Seychelles revoked overflight privileges for Lai’s aircraft.

Although details remain scarce, the Taiwanese government has claimed that the Chinese government threatened to revoke debt cancellation for these countries if they allowed the passage of Lai’s aircraft. It is possible that China may have exercised similar leverage over Pakistan. If so, this would suggest that restricting Taiwan’s access to airspace has become a new tactic in China’s playbook for pressuring Taiwan.

For its part, the Lai administration has sought to link Pakistan’s actions to Taiwan’s exclusion from the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the United Nations body responsible for global aviation safety. Taiwanese governments have long called for Taiwan’s admission to the ICAO, raising the dangers for international aviation safety when a large aviation hub such as Taiwan is excluded from the global body for civil aviation.

It is also possible that the Pakistan government revoked overflight privileges for EVA Air and China Airlines of its own initiative as a means of strengthening ties with Beijing. For countries that wish to build stronger ties with China, hitting out at Taiwan is a way to signal their dedication to Beijing.

In the same way, vocal support for Taiwan can be used to signal a desire for closer ties with the United States. For instance, the governments of countries in Eastern Europe such as Lithuania showed support for Taiwan through actions such as donating vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic as part of broader signaling efforts to indicate alignment with the United States, its Western European allies, and NATO.

Pakistan claimed that its actions were in compliance with its One China policy. Chinese government rhetoric implies the existence of a unitary One China policy or One China principle as an international consensus – sometimes with the claim that this was codified in international law by way of U.N. Resolution 2758. Citing the One China policy or One China principle has become for China to justify any number of moves against Taiwan. In reality, each country has a different and distinctive One China policy.

China often attempts to create the perception that it is already internationally recognized as having sovereignty over Taiwan. Chinese embassies abroad have sometimes been accused of seeking to take credit for the actions of the Taiwanese representative offices in assisting Taiwanese citizens with repatriation or evacuation. Taiwan maintains representative offices – often termed economic and cultural offices – in lieu of embassies in countries that it does not have formal relations with. Attempting to take credit for such actions would be a means of asserting that China’s embassies are internationally recognized as responsible for Taiwanese citizens abroad.

China has used incidents of Taiwanese nationals being extradited to China similarly. Taiwanese nationals are sometimes extradited to China to face charges because they committed acts of fraud against Chinese citizens. Beijing uses such cases to try to depict the international justice system as considering Taiwan part of China.

At times, China’s efforts have been used to intimidate. For example, last year, during a period that saw trips to Europe by a number of prominent Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) politicians, the Chinese government attempted to create the perception that it would arrest DPP legislator and current Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen during Shen’s travels in Europe through Interpol. The Chinese government also claimed to have a criminal investigation on Shen ongoing in Chongqing. For its part, Interpol stated that it would not act on political disputes. Nevertheless, China has routinely been accused of seeking to weaponize Interpol “red notices” in order to target political dissidents.

Attempting to push for the revocation of overflight privileges for Taiwanese airlines, however, would be a new tactic for China. It’s worth watching to see if Pakistan ever actually institutes such a ban, and if other countries decide to follow suit.
